questions.stem: A client with an acute asthma exacerbation has received repeated inhaled bronchodilator therapy. The client is now drowsy, speaks only single words, has minimal air movement, and the oxygen saturation is falling. What should the nurse do?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Continue the same intermittent treatment schedule and reassess in one hour because reduced wheezing usually indicates that bronchospasm is resolving.","B":"Escalate emergency respiratory care immediately, continue acute asthma treatment, and prepare for advanced airway support if respiratory failure progresses.","C":"Have the client walk to improve ventilation and obtain a peak-flow value before notifying the provider, because objective testing should precede escalation.","D":"Withhold supplemental oxygen until an arterial blood gas is obtained because oxygen can obscure the severity of airflow obstruction during assessment."}}
questions.rationale: Drowsiness, inability to speak normally, worsening hypoxemia, and markedly reduced air movement during an asthma exacerbation are high-risk features for impending respiratory failure. Current GINA guidance requires urgent escalation and intensive treatment rather than delayed reassessment or exertional testing. Supplemental oxygen should not be withheld from a hypoxemic patient.
questions.source_name: Global Initiative for Asthma — 2026 GINA Strategy Report
questions.source_detail: 2026 GINA guidance covers acute severe asthma and urgent escalation when clinical features indicate life-threatening exacerbation or impending respiratory failure.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a new parent about infant feeding. According to WHO recommendations, exclusive breastfeeding is recommended for approximately the first how many months of life?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"6 months","B":"It is not recommended at all","C":"12 months","D":"2 months"}}
questions.rationale: The World Health Organization recommends exclusive breastfeeding for approximately the first 6 months of life, with continued breastfeeding alongside appropriate complementary foods recommended up to 2 years of age or beyond.
questions.source_name: World Health Organization — Infant and Young Child Feeding Guidance

questions.stem: A nurse conducting a well-child visit for a toddler should prioritize screening for which of the following, per standard pediatric preventive care recommendations?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Adult chronic disease risk factors only","B":"Retirement planning discussion with parents","C":"Developmental milestones and growth parameters","D":"Occupational exposure history"}}
questions.rationale: Well-child visits focus on age-appropriate screening including developmental milestones (motor, language, social), growth parameters (height, weight, head circumference), and immunization status, per Bright Futures/AAP preventive care guidelines.
questions.source_name: American Academy of Pediatrics — Bright Futures Guidelines

questions.stem: A client with a 20-year smoking history states, "I know smoking is bad for me, but I'm not ready to quit right now," during a visit where the nurse had planned to discuss setting a quit date. According to the Transtheoretical (Stages of Change) Model, this client's statement suggests they are actually in which stage, and how should the nurse adjust the visit's focus?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Contemplation, so the nurse should focus on exploring ambivalence rather than setting a specific quit date yet","B":"Recognize the client as ready to commit to a specific quit date and proceed with the originally planned action-oriented visit","C":"Recognize the client as not yet aware that smoking poses any health risk, despite the client's own comment acknowledging the risk","D":"Recognize the client as having already quit and needing relapse-prevention support instead of a cessation conversation"}}
questions.rationale: The Contemplation stage is characterized by awareness of the problem behavior and its consequences, but not yet being ready to take action to change it — distinct from Precontemplation (not yet considering change) or Preparation (actively planning to change soon).
questions.source_name: Prochaska & DiClemente — Transtheoretical Model of Behavior Change

questions.stem: A client who is angry about their diagnosis states to the nurse, "You don't care about me at all," despite the nurse having spent extra time providing attentive, unhurried care throughout the shift. This statement may reflect which defense mechanism?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Recognize the statement as the client offering a logical, face-saving explanation for their own difficult feelings","B":"Recognize the statement as the client channeling an unacceptable urge into a socially productive outlet","C":"Projection, in which the client attributes their own difficult feelings onto the nurse rather than acknowledging them directly","D":"Recognize the statement as the client reverting to communication patterns typical of an earlier developmental stage"}}
questions.rationale: Projection is a defense mechanism in which a person attributes their own unacceptable feelings or thoughts (such as the client's own distress or fear) onto another person. Recognizing this helps the nurse respond therapeutically rather than personally.
questions.source_name: Psychiatric-Mental Health Nursing Foundations — Ego Defense Mechanisms

questions.stem: A nurse is using the SOLER technique to demonstrate active listening with a distressed client. What does the "L" in SOLER represent?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Listen without interrupting","B":"Leave when appropriate","C":"Look away to give privacy","D":"Lean toward the client"}}
questions.rationale: The SOLER technique for nonverbal active listening stands for: Sit facing the client, Open posture, Lean toward the client, Eye contact (appropriate), and Relax. Leaning toward the client conveys attentiveness and engagement.
questions.source_name: Egan, G. — The Skilled Helper (widely referenced counseling communication framework)

questions.stem: When documenting and discussing care for a client with a substance use disorder, the nurse should use which type of language, per current best practice?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Judgmental language that clearly emphasizes personal responsibility for the seriousness of the condition","B":"Person-first, non-stigmatizing language (e.g., \"a person with a substance use disorder\" rather than labeling terms)","C":"Informal labels such as 'addict' or 'abuser,' since these terms are widely understood among staff members","D":"Avoiding any mention of the substance use disorder in documentation, to protect the client's confidentiality"}}
questions.rationale: Current best practice, reflected in guidance from SAMHSA and professional nursing organizations, recommends person-first, non-stigmatizing language when discussing substance use disorders, since stigmatizing terms can negatively affect client care and treatment-seeking behavior.
questions.source_name: SAMHSA — Words Matter: Terminology to Reduce Stigma
questions.source_detail: Person-First Language for Substance Use Disorders
